opening.headline: Understand the reason why 429 is displayed every time there is a lot of traffic in terms of the unit and structure of the limit, and decide whether to increase it or avoid it through design.
body: Services that normally run well may issue a 429 error right after an event. When a large number of requests are received at once, some are successful and some are rejected with 429 Too Many Requests. Users sometimes feel like it doesn't work, and retrying failed requests increases traffic again, creating a vicious cycle.

In this class, you will learn what rate limits are measured in, how usage tiers and quotas raise the limits, and which services require reserved throughput. And practice choosing the appropriate response to the situation by distinguishing between ways to raise the limit and ways to avoid it through design.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the concepts of rate limit, quota, and throughput allocation
You can distinguish between ways to raise limits and ways to avoid them through design.
429 Can explain the basics of retry, such as exponential backoff, jitter, Retry-After, and the limit operation of the token bucket method.

screens.title: Whenever there is a lot of traffic, 429 comes up.
screens.lead: Read what happened at one service right after the event. It's helpful to note how errors lead to a vicious cycle.

visual.alt: A graph showing the number of requests over time, the limit line, and 429 occurring in sections exceeding the limit.

paragraphs: Customer service chatbots operate reliably throughout the day. However, as inquiries poured in immediately after the promotional email was sent, some requests were successful and others were rejected with 429 Too Many Requests. The same user also experienced a situation where sometimes it works and sometimes it doesn't.

Sometimes the user feels like it doesn't work, and the app sends the failed request right back. This retry again causes traffic to exceed the limit, resulting in more 429s. Once started, the vicious cycle can continue until traffic dwindles.

In this situation, the team is faced with a two-pronged choice. Should I ask for the limit to be raised, or should I change my request method to avoid reaching the limit? Which one is correct depends on how the limit is set.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: When you get a 429, is it always best to ask for your limit to be raised right away? I'll answer again at the end of class.

screens.outro: First, let me recall an experience I had when I was pushed to my limit.

screens.title: Think back: The moment you hit your limit
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever received a 429 while running a large task?
items.answer: Bulk operations tend to send a lot of requests in a short period of time, often hitting the limit. At this time, rather than simply waiting or sending again, you can find the cause and solution by knowing what unit the limit is set in.

items.prompt: Have you ever been confused as to whether the limit is due to the number of requests or the number of tokens?
items.answer: The limit is made up of multiple units measuring the number of requests and number of tokens, so it is difficult to tell which limit has been reached. Response headers and how to check the remaining amount in the dashboard are covered in this lesson.

items.prompt: How did you handle retries after errors?
items.answer: Immediate retries are a common cause of vicious cycles. The default is exponential backoff, which increases the interval and respects the latency announced by the server.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's start by checking the units of the limit.

screens.title: RPM and TPM: units of rate limit
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation appears. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: Rate limiting is implemented across multiple units. RPM represents requests per minute, TPM represents tokens per minute, and RPD represents daily request count. OpenAI also includes TPD (daily tokens) and IPM (images per minute) in these limits. If any of these limits are exceeded, an error occurs. For example, if RPM is set to 20, even if TPM remains available, the 21st request will be rejected. Gemini's limit is defined by project unit and is not per API key; OpenAI uses organizational limits defined by project unit. Both services have different values per model. Claude's rate limit types are divided into requests_per_minute, input_tokens_per_minute, and output_tokens_per_minute. A 429 error indicates that requests were sent too rapidly, while a 503 error indicates that the server temporarily cannot accept requests. When a 429 error occurs, check the response headers and the remaining quota in the dashboard. OpenAI provides Retry-After and the x-ratelimit series of headers.

terms.tip: There is a limit on the number of requests per minute. No matter how small the token is, if the number of requests is high, this limit will be reached.
There is a limit on the number of tokens per minute. If your request sends at least long inputs and outputs, this limit may be reached first.
Daily request limit. Even if it is within the minute limit, if the total daily amount is exceeded, it will be rejected.
Gemini's limits are per-project and not per-API key. Even if you create multiple keys for the same project, the limit will be exhausted.

This is an HTTP standard header that tells the server how long to wait before requesting again. It is not a feature of any particular service; the value is either an integer in seconds or a date format. It may be included in a 429 or 503 response, but is not always present. When present, it must be respected as a minimum waiting time.

screens.title: 429 Retry Basics: Exponential Backoff, Jitter, Token Bucket
screens.lead: When you select each item, an explanation will unfold. When you receive a 429, open it one by one to find out how to resend it and how the limit is filled.

visual.alt: A two-line timetable where retries at equal intervals cause a rush of requests, and adding jitter causes them to disperse.
labels: All clients retry at the same moment

items.title: 429 and 503, and Retry-After
items.body: 429 Too Many Requests is defined in the standard (RFC 6585) as sending too many requests in a given period of time. How a server identifies a user and counts requests is not set by a standard and is left up to the service. 503 Service Unavailable means in the HTTP standard (RFC 9110) that the server is currently unable to process due to temporary overload or maintenance. Both allow the server to tell how long to wait with a Retry-After header, which is an HTTP standard and not a feature of any particular service. The value is either an integer in seconds or a date format. Not all 429s have this header, so you also need a way to handle it when it doesn't.

items.title: Why immediate retries create a vicious cycle
items.body: If requests that exceed the limit fail all at once, many clients will resend at the same moment. These retries push the limit again, creating more failures, and worse, since failed requests are also included in the limit calculation. This phenomenon of a rush of requests at the same time is commonly called a thundering herd. The purpose of the retry is not to send again quickly, but to give the server time to recover.

items.title: Exponential backoff
items.body: This method doubles the waiting time with each retry. For example, increase it to 1 second, 2 seconds, 4 seconds, and 8 seconds. Make the first retry quickly, but as failures continue, take longer breaks to reduce the burden on the server. We put an upper limit on the maximum waiting time and the maximum number of attempts to prevent them from increasing indefinitely, and also put an upper limit on the total time spent on retries. If the SDK and the application each retry, the number of attempts will be doubled, so turn off retries on one side or limit them by combining them.

items.title: Jitter: Randomness that disrupts latency
items.body: If you only use exponential backoff, clients that start at the same time will retry at the same time, and there will still be a rush of requests. Jitter adds a random value to the latency to stagger the timing of retries. A typical method, full jitter, randomly picks between 0 and the current exponential latency. In pseudocode, it is written as `sleep = random(0, min(maximum value, standard value * 2^number of attempts))`. One engineering article summarized that adding jitter in high-contention situations significantly reduces the total number of calls and completion times, and that jitter can be viewed as a standard approach for remote clients. When the server gives Retry-After, we take that value as the minimum wait time and add a small random delay on top of it.

items.title: Is the limit a minute window or a continuously filling bucket?
items.body: The names RPM or TPM make it sound like the limits are reset every minute. However, some services use the token bucket method. Buckets contain available capacity, requests consume capacity, and capacity is continuously refilled over time until it is maxed out. It is not reset all at once at a fixed time. Claude's article explains this approach, noting that the limit of 60 per minute can effectively be enforced at once per second, so short bursts can push the limit. Since implementation varies from service to service, check the documentation of the service you are using.

items.title: Reasons to look at peaks rather than averages
items.body: From a bucket perspective, limits are a matter of instantaneous consumption rate and remaining capacity, not average usage. Even if your daily average is half the limit, if you overflow for a few seconds, the bucket will empty and you will get 429. The OpenAI document explains that even if the usage is within the limit, 429 (slow_down) may occur if traffic increases too quickly, and the Claude document also advises to increase it gradually as the acceleration limit may be hit if the usage increases rapidly. So the solution is not just to raise the limit, but also rate control to even out requests, jittered retries, and gradual increases.

screens.outro: Now that you know how retries and limits work, let's take a step-by-step look at how limits are raised.

screens.title: Usage Tier: Structure with increasing limits
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to see step by step how usage tiers for each service increase the limit.

visual.alt: A staircase diagram in which tiers increase and limits increase according to cumulative payments.
labels: Automatically increases with accumulated credit purchases

steps.title: Tiers of Gemini
steps.body: Gemini has free and usage tiers from Tier 1 to Tier 3. Cumulative payments and elapsed time are criteria for eligibility. As the tier goes up, the limit increases, so the limit is gradually opened as you advance the service.

steps.title: Spending Based Limits
steps.body: Gemini has spend-based limits in a 10-minute rolling window that are independent of RPM and TPM. If this limit is exceeded, 429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED will be returned. This means that if you use a lot of expensive models with a small number of requests or tokens, it can get caught.

steps.title: Tiers of OpenAI
steps.body: OpenAI's paid tiers are Build, Launch, and Grow, which automatically increase when your accumulated credit purchases reach the threshold. The characteristic is that the limit is opened based on purchase history without application or screening.

steps.title: Values are different for each model
steps.body: As tiers increase, model-specific limits generally increase. However, the values ​​vary by model, so you should check your dashboard to see the actual values ​​for your organization. It is important to get into the habit of checking general numbers rather than memorizing them.

steps.title: Plan your climbing time as well.
steps.body: Tiers have conditions such as cumulative payments and elapsed periods, so they may not go up right away when you need them. If you're expecting a surge in traffic, such as a big event or launch, it's a safe bet to check your limits a few days in advance and, if necessary, request a raise or adjust your design in advance. The limit is the value you see before the surge, not after.

steps.title: Queue limits for batches
steps.body: OpenAI Batch counts waiting input tokens as a queue limit. Once the placement is complete, those tokens are taken out of the limit. Batch has a separate high limit from the real-time limit, so you can save on the real-time limit by moving jobs that tolerate delays.

screens.outro: Now that you understand tiers, let’s see how to read the quotas on your cloud platform.

screens.title: How to read quotas and limits
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn how to read your cloud platform's quotas and limits.

tabs.label: Defaults and system limits
tabs.body: Quotas in Agent Platform have default values and can usually be adjusted. On the other hand, system limits are fixed and cannot be changed. When you encounter a limit, the first thing to distinguish is whether it is an adjustable quota or a fixed system limit. If it is a system limit, it will not change even if requested, so it must be solved by design.

tabs.label: project level
tabs.body: Quotas are usually at the project level. Usage in one project does not affect quotas in other projects. So, dividing projects by environment or team prevents congestion in one area from spreading to other areas.

tabs.label: When the limit is reached
tabs.body: If the limit is reached, access will most likely be blocked and the operation will fail. It's not slowed down, it's rejected. Therefore, you should proactively monitor your resource consumption and receive notifications when you approach your limit. If you react after the limit has been reached, the user will have already seen the error.

tabs.label: Claude Rate Limits API
tabs.body: The Rate Limits API allows you to programmatically read the limits set for your organization and workspace. The read values ​​can be used to synchronize the gateway or written to notifications. Workspace limits have a source that tells you whether they are overridden by your workspace or inherited by your organization.

screens.outro: Now that you know how to read limits, let's compare the throughput of reservation methods.

screens.title: Provisioned Throughput and Throughput Quotas
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare the difference between pay-as-you-go and reserved capacity.

states.label: pay as you go
states.body: This is the default method of Agent Platform. You only pay for what you use, there are no contracts. Variants like Priority and Flex allow you to control cost and performance. Because it uses public resources, it may be subject to limits or congestion during peak hours. It is suitable for services with irregular or small traffic. The usual order is to initially start with a pay-as-you-go system, observe usage patterns, and then decide whether to make a reservation.

states.label: Provisioned Throughput
states.body: A fixed-cost, fixed-duration subscription that reserves throughput by specific model and location. Ideal when you need real-time services like chatbots or agents, consistently high throughput, consistent user experience, and predictable costs. OpenAI Reserved Tier also purchases capacity in advance on a per-minute basis, and usage beyond the limit is paid as you go. If your usage doesn't consistently fill your reserved capacity, you're wasting money. Always keep in mind that reservations cost money even when you don't use them. You can also start a little smaller by sizing your reservations based on peaks and durations rather than averages, and taking advantage of the fact that excesses are pay-as-you-go.

screens.outro: Now that you have seen all the concepts, let’s solve the surge traffic example step by step.

screens.title: Explanatory example: Conditions for needing reserved throughput in surge traffic
screens.lead: The instructor explains the case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: I have a customer service chatbot that gets a lot of requests at certain times of the day. Inquiries are concentrated during lunch hours and right after work, and it is quiet at other times. Errors usually appear during rush hours.

steps.title: Step 1: Check for symptoms
steps.body: During peak times, the TPM limit will be exceeded and a 429 will be displayed and the user will see the error. Check which limit was reached first using response headers and a dashboard. It may be due to the number of tokens rather than the number of requests.

steps.title: Step 2: Calculate by peak
steps.body: Calculate peak RPM and TPM, not average, and compare to limits. On average per day, it may be less than half of the limit, but if there are a few peak minutes that exceed the limit, an error will occur during that time.

steps.title: Step 3: Review reservation throughput
steps.body: If peaks are long, recurring, and real-time response is essential, review scheduled throughput. Chatbots make users wait, making it difficult to queue them up and process them late. In this case, it is appropriate to secure throughput through reservations.

steps.title: Step 4: If your reservation does not match
steps.body: For tasks that have rare peaks or can tolerate delays, use queuing and batching instead of scheduling. Reservations are a fixed cost, so if you don't use them consistently, they're a waste. Consider whether it is cost-effective to reserve full capacity due to peaks.

steps.title: conclusion
steps.body: This chatbot is a candidate for scheduled throughput because it is real-time and has recurring peaks. Conversely, if nightly report generation is using the same limit, move it to a batch first. However, if you change the retry method to exponential backoff before making a reservation and reduce token consumption through caching, the required reservation size itself will be reduced.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the conditions that require a reservation, let's compare when to raise the limit and when to avoid it.

data.notes: Judgment comes down to one thing. If the limit is structurally insufficient, it is raised, and if it is a temporary surge or waste, it is solved through design. First, reducing avoidable waste through design reduces the amount of limit you have to raise. It is common to review the bottom four rows of the table before the top rows because they are less expensive and can be tried right away. The two directions are not exclusive and are often used together.

screens.outro: Now that we have summarized the criteria for judgment, let’s gather the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Expand items to see evidence
screens.lead: When you select each item, the basis for the summary statement will unfold. There is nothing to enter or submit.

items.title: The rate limit is measured in several units such as RPM and TPM, and if any one is exceeded, it becomes 429.
items.body: The number of requests, number of tokens, and daily total each have limits. Even if there are enough tokens, requests will be rejected if the number of requests exceeds the limit. Check the response headers and dashboard to see what your limits are.

items.title: Limits can be raised by adjusting tiers and quotas.
items.body: Usage tiers increase with cumulative payments or credit purchases, and quotas on cloud platforms can usually be requested to be adjusted. However, the system limit is fixed. Tiers and quotas have different values ​​for each model, so you'll need to check your values ​​in the dashboard.

items.title: Reserved throughput is a means of securing recurring peaks in real-time services.
items.body: Provisioned Throughput is a fixed-cost subscription that reserves throughput by specific model and location. OpenAI Reserved Tier is similar, with excess paid on a pay-as-you-go basis.

items.title: Designs such as backoff, queuing, batching, and caching reduce hitting limits.
items.body: Fixing the retry scheme, sending requests flat, moving tasks around to tolerate delays, and reducing token consumption can solve the problem without raising the limit.

screens.title: Connect to my work
screens.lead: This screen is for reading only. Read the questions and think for yourself. You will not enter or submit an answer.

paragraphs: Key terms in this lesson are RPM and TPM, usage tiers, quotas, and Provisioned Throughput. Let's go back to the original question. When you get a 429, is it always best to ask for your limit to be raised right away?

That's not true. First, you need to determine which limit you've hit and whether it's a structural shortage or a temporary surge or waste. If you solve a problem that can be solved through design by raising the limit, the cost will only increase and the same problem will arise again.

Think about the peak hours of your service. You can check that you know the RPMs and TPMs at peaks rather than averages, that retries are immediate, and that tasks that tolerate delays are using the same limits.
Next, check to see if the limit is insufficient even after reducing everything that can be reduced by design. Only then can you decide which tier, quota, or reserved throughput is right for you.

callout.label: Questions to Think About
callout.text: Where do I get stuck with RPM and TPM in my work? If you get 429 on the service now, guess which limit will be reached first.

checks.q: In a model with an RPM limit of 20, the TPM sent the 21st request within one minute, even though there was still a lot left. What are the results?
options: It is rejected. If any one of the limits is exceeded, an error occurs.
Since there is TPM remaining, it is processed normally.
It is processed, but the unit price goes up.
The server automatically waits until the next person and then processes it.
checks.explain: The limit is measured in several units such as RPM and TPM, and if any one is exceeded, error 429 is generated. Even if there is room for tokens, the limit on the number of requests is separate.

wrong.1: Each limit is applied separately, so margins on one do not supersede the other.
wrong.2: Exceeding the limit will result in a rejection rather than a unit price.
wrong.3: The server does not automatically wait and a 429 rejection is returned.

checks.intro: When the limit applies to multiple units, check what happens if just one is exceeded.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. The limit is measured by units such as RPM and TPM, and if any one is exceeded, an error occurs and the token is rejected regardless of token margin.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Even though TPM remains, RPM is a separate limit. Remember that if any of the limits are exceeded you will receive a 429 error.

checks.q: Which of the following is an appropriate description of Agent Platform's quotas?
options: As one project's usage increases, other projects' quotas also become depleted.
System limits can also be raised by requesting an adjustment.
When the limit is reached, the operation continues to succeed and the speed gradually slows down.
Quotas have default values and can usually be adjusted, and project usage does not affect each other.
checks.explain: Quotas are generally at the project level, so adjustments can be requested without affecting each other. The system limit is fixed and cannot be changed, and access is blocked in most cases when the limit is reached, so monitor it in advance.

wrong.0: There is no impact between projects.
wrong.2: When the limit is reached, most access is blocked and the operation fails.

checks.intro: Make sure you know exactly what your quota is and whether it can be adjusted.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. Quotas are usually at the project level so they do not affect each other and the default values ​​can usually be requested to be adjusted.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Exhaust is not shared between projects, system limits are fixed, and access is blocked in most cases when the limit is reached. Double-check your views based on these three things.

checks.q: Match the appropriate responses to the following situations:
left: The average usage is half of the limit, but there is occasionally a temporary surge in requests.
Peaks are long and repetitive, and real-time response is essential.
Bulk operations that tolerate delays eat up real-time limits
right: Request a usage tier increase or quota increase
Mitigated by exponential backoff retry and request queuing
Move to batch or Flex and subtract from real-time limit
checks.explain: If the limit is structurally insufficient, it is raised, and temporary surges or waste are resolved through design. Reserved throughput makes sense for real-time services with long, recurring peaks.
checks.intro: The solution to the limit problem varies depending on the cause. Match the situation with the response.
checks.correctFeedback: That's correct. Temporary surges and waste were resolved through design, and structural shortages were distinguished by raising limits.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There is a mismatched pair. Backoff and queuing are appropriate for temporary surges, reserved throughput is appropriate for repeated long peaks, separation of delay-tolerant tasks into batches or flex, and expansion requests are appropriate for structural shortages.

glossary.def: Limits on the number of requests per minute and the number of tokens per minute. If you exceed even one, you get 429.
This is the stage where the limit is increased automatically or approved depending on accumulated spending or payment history.
This is the upper limit of resources that the project can use. Defaults can be adjusted upon request and system limits are fixed.

Provisioned Throughput is a fixed-cost, fixed-term subscription that reserves throughput by specifying a model and location. Throughput quota is a limit system that determines whether throughput is secured through pay-as-you-go or reserved capacity.
This is an HTTP standard header that tells the server how long to wait for the client. This may be included in a 429 or 503 response, and if present, will follow with the minimum waiting time.

Exponential backoff is a method of gradually increasing the retry interval, and jitter is a method of adding a random value to the waiting time to prevent retries from being concentrated at one point.

misconceptions.fact: This is usually a sign that a limit such as RPM or TPM has been exceeded. It's not that the service is broken, it's a matter of request method and limits.

misconceptions.myth: If you have tokens left, you will not be subject to the request limit.
misconceptions.fact: If just one of the limits is exceeded, it will be rejected. If the RPM is 20, the 21st request will be rejected even if there is TPM remaining.

misconceptions.myth: The limit is different for each API key.
misconceptions.fact: Gemini's limits are per project, while OpenAI's limits are per organization and per project. Increasing the height does not increase the limit.

misconceptions.myth: If you receive a 429, sending it back immediately is the fastest way to recover.
misconceptions.fact: Immediate retry pushes requests back over the limit at the same time, and even failed requests are counted toward the limit. It sticks to the latency advertised by the server, and adds jitter to the exponential backoff to increase the spacing and spread it out.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The rate limit is measured in several units such as RPM and TPM, and if any one is exceeded, it becomes 429.
You can increase the limit by adjusting tiers and quotas.
Reserved throughput is a means of securing recurring peaks in real-time services.
Designs like backoff, queuing, batching, and caching reduce hitting limits.
